learningObjective: Explain why deep-learning runtimes use a caching memory allocator (a pool of previously freed device blocks) instead of calling cudaMalloc/cudaFree per tensor.

canonicalClaims.claim: A caching allocator pools freed device blocks in size-classed buckets and reuses them, avoiding the microsecond-to-millisecond cost and cross-stream synchronization implied by cudaMalloc/cudaFree, at the cost of managing fragmentation.
conditions: Workload performs frequent allocations/frees per step.
The runtime has visibility into all device allocations to coordinate reuse.
nonImplications: Does not imply memory can never be returned to the OS; empty-cache APIs exist.

misconceptions.claim: cudaMalloc returns memory that must be initialized before use.
misconceptions.whyWrong: cudaMalloc'd memory is usable as a kernel argument; contents are uninitialized but usable.

misconceptions.claim: There is a 1024-allocation limit per process.
misconceptions.whyWrong: No such limit exists in the CUDA runtime; the limit is device memory.
They mitigate fragmentation but cannot eliminate it; long-running workloads may still OOM due to fragmentation.
cudaFree synchronizes and is expensive; that's why runtimes cache blocks.
